q-343939.worked_solution:
The infimum of $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B,$ and the supremum is the smallest upper bound of $B.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

Since $B$ is unbounded below, $B$ has no lower bounds, so $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Next, to find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge \sqrt{2}$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $[\sqrt{2},\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x<\sqrt{2}$ is **not** an upper bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, $[\sqrt{2},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $B,$ and

$$
sup(B)=min\,[\sqrt{2},\infty )=\sqrt{2}.
$$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of a set $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B,$ and the supremum is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $B.$

Since $B$ is $\text{unbounded below},$ we have $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Since $B$ is $\text{bounded above},$ we have $sup(B)=\sqrt{2}.$

q-253840.problem:
Consider the following set.

$$
A=\{1+3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n}\,:\,n\in N\}
$$

For this set, we have that {{field-1}}.
q-253840.worked_solution:
The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=1+3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14163598/assets/198c3d6737439fcfa204926394b317aae0026502b5eaacb9e2f0429941f23db3.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing and converges to $1.$ The maximum of $A$ is 

$$
max(A)={a}_{1}=1+3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{1}=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\ge {a}_{1}$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $x<{a}_{1}$ cannot be an upper bound because ${a}_{1},$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $x.$

Therefore, $[\frac{7}{4},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
sup(A)=min[\frac{7}{4},\infty )=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

Notice that $\frac{7}{4}$ is the maximum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

$$
sup(A)=\frac{7}{4}\in A.
$$

Consider the following set. A={1+3(14)n:n∈N}For this set, we have that
sup(A)=74∈A

sup(A)=1∈A
sup(A)=74∈A
sup(A)=1∉A

EXPLANATION

The supremum of a set A is the smallest upper bound of A.

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing all upper bounds of A (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of A are the terms of the sequence an, given by

an=1+3(14)n,n∈N={1,2,3,4,…}.

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

We see that an is decreasing and converges to 1. The maximum of A is max(A)=a1=1+3(14)1=74.

So, in our case, we have that

  • any number x≥a1 is an upper bound of A,

  • any number x<a1 cannot be an upper bound because a1, an element of A, is greater than x.

Therefore, [74,∞) is the set of upper bounds of A, and

sup(A)=min[74,∞)=74.

Notice that 74 is the maximum of A. Therefore, we conclude that

sup(A)=74∈A.

q-253911.worked_solution:
The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=(-1)^{n}\cdot (n-1),\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14163598/assets/5812e3dd22994d613ecc84087418cddfa978e98c1324869f290e1bf2b1317bad.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is an oscillating, non-convergent sequence. Moreover, $A$ is unbounded above. In other words, for any real number $x,$ we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ such that ${a}_{n}$ is greater than $x.$ Therefore, $A$ has no upper bounds and $sup(A)=+\infty .$

{{field-1}}
q-253853.worked_solution:
The infimum of a function is the infimum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=[-1,3].$

To find the infimum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\le -1$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $y>-1$ is **not** a lower bound of $A$ because $-1,$ an element of $A,$ is smaller than $y.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{inf}_{x\in R}f(x)=inf(A)=max(-\infty ,-1]=-1.
$$
